headline: Ebola Surges in DRC as Outbreak Hits 60 Zones, Health Minister Calls It Worst in History
deck: Two new health zones have fallen to the virus, expanding a crisis already straining the country’s fragile health system.
body: The Ebola outbreak tearing through eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has surged into two fresh zones, raising the total number of affected areas to 60, according to Al Jazeera and AP News. Health officials confirm the geographic expansion marks one of the most rapid escalations in a crisis that health minister Dr. Jean-Jacques Muyembe has declared the country’s worst on record. The World Health Organization’s second meeting of the International Health Regulations Emergency Committee underscores the alarm gripping global health circles. For a nation already grappling with years of conflict and under-resourced infrastructure, this latest surge signals a crisis deepening by the day.

The spread into new zones comes as Congo begins mass vaccinations to blunt the outbreak’s advance. Health authorities launched the campaign this week, a move described by PBS as a necessary but belated attempt to catch up with the virus’s relentless march. The vaccinations target high-risk communities, healthcare workers, and contacts of confirmed cases, aiming to create firebreaks before transmission spirals further. Yet even as vials of experimental vaccines reach clinics, the virus continues to outpace containment efforts, fueled by porous borders and deep community distrust of health interventions.

The scale of the disaster is staggering. Sixty health zones now report cases or exposure, a figure that has doubled since the outbreak’s start and stretches from urban clinics to remote villages along the Rwanda and Uganda borders. Analysts tracking the spread describe it as the fastest-growing Ebola epidemic in modern history, a designation that carries ominous implications for regional stability. Each new zone represents not just a geographic expansion but a failure to halt transmission in areas where families live in close quarters and burial rituals risk accelerating the virus’s spread.

The health minister’s admission that this is the worst outbreak in DRC’s history reflects the sheer brutality of the current strain. Unlike previous epidemics, which were largely contained in remote areas, this one has infiltrated bustling towns and cities, where dense populations and constant movement defy quarantine. The WHO’s emergency committee meeting last week reflected the gravity, with experts weighing whether to declare a Public Health Emergency of International Concern—a designation that could unlock additional resources but also risk stigmatizing the region.

Vaccinations offer a glimmer of hope, but their impact remains uncertain. Supplies of the Ervebo vaccine are limited, and logistical hurdles in a country with crumbling roads and intermittent electricity complicate distribution. Health workers report that misinformation and resistance in communities—fueled by rumors that vaccines are part of a foreign plot—have stalled uptake. One nurse in Goma told AP News that despite repeated awareness campaigns, villagers refuse doses, fearing the needle itself will infect them.

The outbreak’s acceleration has exposed the fragility of Congo’s health system, already buckling under the weight of decades of conflict and underfunding. International aid groups warn that without a dramatic increase in funding and personnel, the virus will continue to exploit every weakness. Médecins Sans Frontières has warned that the current trajectory mirrors the early stages of the 2014 West Africa outbreak, which eventually killed more than 11,000 people. The parallel is chilling for a country that has already buried thousands of its own citizens.

Meanwhile, the World Health Organization is urging neighboring countries to heighten surveillance along their borders with DRC. Uganda and Rwanda have stepped up screenings at official crossings, but porous informal routes remain a major risk. Health officials in both countries have reported isolated cases linked to cross-border travel, raising fears that the virus could leapfrog containment zones if left unchecked. The WHO’s emergency committee is expected to reconvene in the coming weeks to reassess the situation and determine whether a global alarm is warranted.

For now, the focus remains on containment. Health workers are racing against time to trace contacts, isolate the sick, and vaccinate the vulnerable, but the odds are steep. The outbreak’s spread to 60 zones proves the virus respects no borders—geographic or political. As one epidemiologist put it, 'Ebola doesn’t need visas. It moves with people.' The question is whether Congo’s health system, stretched to its breaking point, can outrun a pathogen that thrives on chaos.
